verdicts.why: Approaching someone with a proposal describes the act of making contact without taking a side on it.
Coming near or verging on something in quality is a plain relation of degree with no attitude attached.
Undergoing training for a role is a neutral description of what a person does, not how the speaker regards it.
Educating someone for a future role is plainly descriptive; there is no plainer neighbour it is loaded against.
Creating by training and teaching describes a process without approval or contempt for it.
Arranging by systematic planning names an activity neutrally; the word passes no judgement on the plan or the planners.
The music-theory sense is a technical term for a harmonic procedure and carries no attitude.
A settled decision is named plainly here; any firmness or desperation in the book sentences comes from surrounding words, not this one.
Pixels per inch is a measurement; the gloss's remark that more is better states a fact about pictures, not an attitude in the word.
Finding a solution to a problem is a neutral description of an outcome, not a verdict on it.
A statement that solves a problem is named without any approval or dismissal beyond its meaning.
The optical sense is a technical measure of an instrument's power and takes no side.
Analysis into components is a plain description of a method with no attitude attached.
The harmonic sense is a technical term for a chord progression and judges nothing.
The medical sense names the subsidence of inflammation in plain clinical terms; a welcome referent is not a loaded word.
The governing body of a nation is named neutrally; any suspicion of the State comes from the speaker's politics, not the word.
Being in a state names agitation informally, but the informality is register and the word is used sympathetically as often as dismissively, so it does not itself take a side.
The territory of a nation is a plain geographical and political term with no attitude.
The chemistry sense names a phase of matter and is purely technical.
Civil as opposed to military is a classifying term with no judgement; the book's polite sense is a different synset and not the one under audit.
A civil year or civil day is a legal-technical classification and carries no attitude.
Soil in which plants grow is named plainly; any judgement of its quality comes from the modifiers, not the noun.
A foundation or basis for something is an abstract relation named without approval or dismissal.
A position won or defended is a neutral spatial-strategic term; it does not judge the side holding it.
The background of a scene is a compositional term with no attitude.
An electrical ground is a purely technical term and judges nothing.
The perceptual ground behind a figure is a term of art in psychology and carries no attitude.
A prepared painting surface is a technical term from art practice with no judgement in it.
A first coat of paint or size is a plain technical term and takes no side.
Increasing in size by natural process is a plain description of change; whatever grows is neither praised nor scorned by the verb.
